compliance.notes: Technically competent, commissioner-overseen TMSS: the core prudential indicators are all present with figures - strongest on capital expenditure/CFR (full year-on-year CFR bridge), the borrowing strategy (clear internal-borrowing/under-borrowing narrative), a properly constructed four-balance liability benchmark chart, the MRP policy statement, and a robust creditworthiness policy using CDS beyond ratings. Weakest area is commercial/non-treasury investment disclosure relative to the size of the legacy 0.9bn book: proportionality is acknowledged but not demonstrated (COM-03 core), the new commercial-income-to-net-revenue indicator is absent (PI-08), and IMPs, the paras 51-53 compliance statement, a quantitative portfolio-risk indicator, an ESG policy, separate HRA/GF benchmarks and an audit-qualification flag are all missing. Overall a compliant recovery-phase strategy whose gaps cluster in the commercial-investment and secondary-disclosure requirements.

news_drafts.headline: Thurrock forecasts £10.3m special needs overspend this year, with deficit projected at £42.5m by 2029
news_drafts.lead:
Thurrock Council forecasts a £10.307m overspend in 2026/27 on its dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools. That is 13% of the £78.560m allocation, according to the first-quarter financial report going to the Children's Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee on 22 October. It would raise the accumulated deficit to £15.226m by 31 March 2027, and the council's DSG management plan projects £42.530m by the end of 2028/29.

The report names the main cause as sustained growth in demand for support for special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), and in the complexity of need. The number of education, health and care plans (legal documents setting out the support a child must receive) funded from the high needs block, the part of school funding for children with SEND, is projected to rise from 2,791 in 2026 to 3,970 by 2029. That is 1,179 more, or 42%. Spending from the block is forecast to grow from £54.342m in 2026/27 to £61.854m in 2028/29.

In February 2026 the government announced that a High Needs Stability Grant will fund 90% of eligible DSG deficits built up to the end of 2025/26, subject to Department for Education approval of a local SEND reform plan. The grant is confirmed only for 2025/26. The report says support is "expected" for 2026/27 and 2027/28. Thurrock must pay the other 10%: £0.492m, £1.031m and £1.217m over those three years, £2.739m in total. The report says the council's medium-term finances depend substantially on whether the support continues beyond 2025/26.

news_drafts.headline: Thurrock commissioners say 2025/26 capital slippage signals "ongoing challenges" on infrastructure
news_drafts.lead:
Commissioners reviewing Thurrock Council have said that capital spending in 2025/26 fell behind its revised budgets, and that this signals "ongoing challenges resulting in potential delay in infrastructure improvements". Capital spending is money spent on things that last, such as buildings and roads. The comment appears in the capital budget summary (Appendix 4) in the papers for the Corporate Overview and Scrutiny Committee, which meets on 8 October 2026.

The slippage is the gap between what the council planned to spend on capital schemes and what it spent. The commissioners said that "stronger governance, stricter oversight on complex capital schemes and effective stakeholder engagement will be essential to improve delivery".

They added that effective governance would be needed to give assurance and to show that decisions were properly informed. The extract does not give the size of the slippage or name the schemes affected.

news_drafts.headline: Thurrock's budget depends on emergency government money as asset sales and building programmes slip.
news_drafts.lead: Thurrock Council set a balanced 2026/27 budget only by assuming £68.9m of exceptional financial support from government — money to cover treasury costs and operational deficit that the council cannot otherwise afford. This emergency backing reveals how deeply the authority depends on two promised routes to financial recovery: selling assets and delivering capital projects. Both are failing. The asset disposal programme is on track to raise only £12.2m of a £25.3m budget, a shortfall of 52%. The capital programme, after slipping £87.5m (73% of budget) in 2025/26, is already forecasting a £15.6m underspend (20% of budget) in the first quarter of the new year. Commissioners, who now oversee the council, have required stronger governance and stricter oversight on complex schemes. The council holds reserves to manage pressures but is drawing them down — £17.9m planned for 2026/27 — rather than closing the underlying gap.

findings.committee: Children's Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Children's Services has delivered 73% of £3.200m savings target by Q1, with remaining 27% on track
findings.detail: The Directorate has delivered £2.320m of its £3.200m savings target by end of Q1 (73%). Major projects delivered include SEN Transport Ad Hoc Routes (£0.300m), Alternative Accommodation Options (£0.300m), Transformation of Children's Social Care operating model (£0.800m), Commissioning (£0.200m), and Review of Education operating model (£0.100m). The remaining £0.880m is on target, primarily from the Review of Placement Options project.
findings.matters: Confirms the council is delivering its planned MTFS mitigation on schedule; savings delivery is critical given demand pressures elsewhere; demonstrates progress on transformation but dependent on continued execution
findings.figures: £3.200m total target; £2.320m delivered by Q1; 73% delivery rate; 27% on track
findings.quote: The Directorate has delivered 73% of its savings at Quarter 1, with the remaining 27% is on target.

findings.committee: Children's Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Children's Services reserves declining from £2.164m to £1.171m, with forecast drawdown of £0.993m in 2026/27
findings.detail: Children's Services reserves are forecast to decline by £0.993m during 2026/27, reducing opening reserves of £2.164m to £1.171m by year-end (a 46% reduction in one year). The drawdown reflects use of ringfenced grant funding and reserves to support service transformation and manage demand pressures. At this rate of drawdown, reserves could be substantially depleted within 2-3 years.
findings.matters: Reserves are a finite and shrinking buffer against further demand growth; rapid depletion limits the council's ability to absorb further pressures or invest in transformation initiatives; indicates reliance on temporary resources rather than budget sustainability
findings.figures: Opening reserves £2.164m; planned drawdown £0.993m; closing reserves £1.171m; drawdown rate 46% in single year
findings.quote: The use of reserves reflects drawdown from reserves of ringfenced grant in line with grant conditions and reflecting the latest Q1 grant returns made.

findings.committee: Children's Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: General Fund demand pressures in placements, NRPF, and aftercare (£0.739m) masked by one-off funding (£0.830m) and staff vacancies (£0.525m)
findings.detail: The General Fund reports a £0.538m underspend, but underlying demand-led pressures total £0.739m: NRPF overspend of £0.133m, Aftercare overspend of £0.386m, and Education overspend of £0.220m. These are offset by one-off funding (£0.317m grants plus £0.513m from reserves) supporting Family Help restructure, staff vacancies (£0.525m), and other underspends. The baseline budget is insufficient for current demand, and mitigation through vacancies and one-off resources is not sustainable.
findings.matters: Once vacancies are filled and one-off funding expires, these pressures will reappear; indicates the budget reset required for transformation has not yet been fully achieved; affects medium-term forecast sustainability
findings.figures: £0.538m underspend; £0.133m NRPF overspend; £0.386m Aftercare overspend; £0.220m Education overspend; £0.830m one-off mitigation; £0.525m vacancy savings
findings.quote: This position reflects a combination of demand-led pressures, particularly within placements support, No Recourse to Public Funds and Aftercare, offset by mitigation through grant maximisation and staffing vacancies.

findings.committee: Children's Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: High Needs Stability Grant expected to cover 90% of historic DSG deficit, confirmed only for 2025/26; Thurrock to fund 10% contribution of £2.739m over three years
findings.detail: Government announced in February 2026 that the High Needs Stability Grant will fund 90% of eligible DSG deficits accrued up to end of 2025/26, subject to DfE approval of a local SEND reform plan. However, the grant is only formally confirmed for 2025/26, with 2026/27 and 2027/28 support described as 'expected' rather than committed. Thurrock must contribute the remaining 10%: £0.492m (2025/26), £1.031m (2026/27), and £1.217m (2027/28), totalling £2.739m.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit management plan is dependent on policy continuation and DfE approval; if support is withdrawn or conditions not met, the council faces an unbudgeted liability; the 10% contribution represents material unfunded cost
findings.figures: 90% grant coverage of historic deficit; 10% council contribution £0.492m + £1.031m + £1.217m = £2.739m over three years
findings.quote: Whilst the High Needs Stability Grant has only been confirmed for 2025/26 it is expected that support will be available to local authorities in 2026/27 and 2027/28.

findings.committee: Children's Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Number of EHCPs funded projected to grow from 2,791 in 2026 to 3,970 by 2029, driving 42% increase in High Needs expenditure
findings.detail: The DSG deficit is driven by sustained growth in demand for SEND provision and complexity of need. Table 8 shows total EHCPs funded by the High Needs Block rising from 2,791 in 2026 to 3,970 by 2029. Corresponding High Needs Block expenditure grows from £54.342m (2026/27) to £61.854m (2028/29). This growth trajectory is both national and local, and shows no sign of moderating within the council's planning period.
findings.matters: Volume growth at this scale creates a self-perpetuating budget challenge; without changes to placement strategy or funding model, DSG deficits will continue and widen even if policy support is extended
findings.figures: 2,791 EHCPs (2026) to 3,970 (2029); growth of 1,179 placements (42%); HNB expenditure £54.342m to £61.854m
findings.quote: This reflects, both the national and local, significant increase in the number of EHCP's and the complexity of need.
